extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, astronomers, and natural philosophers (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Principia Book III (De Mundi Systemate) lays out hypotheses, laws, and propositions that a theory of the solar system must satisfy — methodological principles, observational constraints, and mathematical consequences for planetary motion and gravitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. I — Parsimony of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Causas rerum naturalium non plures admitti debere, quàm quæ & vera sint & earum Phænomenis explicandis sufficiunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natura enim simplex est & rerum causis superfluis non luxuriat. (Principle: do not admit more natural causes than are true and sufficient to explain phenomena.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. II — Uniformity of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideoque effectuum naturalium ejusdem generis eædem sunt causæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: respiration in man and beast; fall of stones in Europe and America; light in candle and Sun; reflection of light on Earth and planets. (Principle: same kinds of natural effects arise from the same kinds of causes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. III — Transformability of bodies / continuity of qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus omne in alterius cujuscunque generis corpus transformari posse, & qualitatum gradus omnes intermedios sucessivè induere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bodies can transform into other kinds and intermediate degrees of qualities exist — used to avoid positing distinct unseen substances when transformations could explain differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. IV — Resting centre of the system
rubrics_metrics.description: Centrum Systematis Mundani quiescere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumed by many: either the Earth or the Sun may be held to rest at the system's center; this is a modelling assumption about the reference center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. V — Areas and periods of Jovian satellites (empirical constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas circumjoviales, radiis ad centrum Jovis ductis, areas describere temporibus proportionales, eorumque tempora periodica esse in ratione sesquialtera distantiarum ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by astronomical observations (Flamsteed, micrometer and eclipses). Table of satellite periods and distances given; observational agreement is required of theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. VI — Five primary planets are solar-orbiting
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas quinque primarios Mercurium, Venerem, Martem, Jovem & Saturnum Orbibus suis Solem cingere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated from their phases (Mercury and Venus show lunar phases; Mars shows full face near conjunction and gibbous at quadrature; Jupiter & Saturn always full-faced) — observational criterion for heliocentrism of these planets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. VII — Kepler's third law for primary planets
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetarum quinque primariorum, & (vel Solis circa Terram vel) Terræ circa Solem tempora periodica esse in ratione sesquialtera mediocrium distantiarum à Sole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kepler's ratio of periods to mean distances is accepted; distances determined by Kepler/Bullialdus and from satellite eclipses; theory must reproduce this relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. VIII — Areas proportional to times about the Sun
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas primarios radiis ad Terram ductis areas describere temporibus minimè proportionales; at radiis ad Solem ductis areas temporibus proportionales percurrere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With respect to Earth planets sometimes appear to retrograde, but with respect to the Sun they progress nearly uniformly so that equal areas are swept in equal times — an observational/theoretical requirement (foundation for heliocentric area law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. IX — Lunar area law
rubrics_metrics.description: Lunam radio ad centrum terræ ducto aream tempori proportionalem describere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent lunar motion compared to apparent diameter indicates the Moon sweeps out areas proportional to time relative to Earth's center; solar perturbations are small and neglected in these hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. I (Theor. I) — Central inverse-square force for Jovian satellites
rubrics_metrics.description: Vires, quibus Planetæ circumjoviales perpetuo retrahuntur à motibus rectilineis & in orbibus suis retinentur, respicere centrum Jovis, & esse reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum locorum ab eodem centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of proof follows from Hypoth. V and earlier propositions. (Criterion: forces retaining satellites are central and vary inversely as square of distance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II (Theor. II) — Central inverse-square force for primary planets (toward Sun)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vires, quibus Planetæ primarii perpetuo retrahuntur à motibus rectilineis, & in Orbibus suis retinentur, respicere Solem, & esse reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Hypoth. VIII and Keplerian relations. Also argued from the near-fixity of aphelia. (Criterion: planetary central force directed to the Sun and inverse-square.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III (Theor. III) — Central inverse-square force for the Moon (toward Earth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vim qua Luna retinetur in Orbe suo respicere terram, & esse reciprocò ut quadratum distantiæ locorum ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Hypoth. IX and lunar apogee motion; deviation is negligible. (Criterion: lunar centripetal force directed to Earth and inverse-square in distance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IV (Theor. IV) — Lunar motion due to Earth's gravity; equivalence of lunar centripetal force and terrestrial gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lunam gravitare in terram, & vi gravitatis retrahi semper à motu rectilineo, & in orbe suo retineri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using lunar distance, period, Earth's radius and pendulum experiments (Huygens), Newton argues the force retaining the Moon is the same force we call gravity at Earth's surface. Includes numerical computations and dependence on assumption that Earth is at rest; if Earth and Moon orbit Sun, slight corrections follow. (Criterion: terrestrial gravity law must extend to lunar distance quantitatively.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V (Theor. V) — Universality of gravitation for planets and satellites
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas circumjoviales gravitare in Jovem, & circumsolares in Solem, & vi gravitatis suæ retrahi semper à motibus rectilineis, & in orbibus curvilineis retineri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolutions of satellites and inner planets are of same kind as Moon about Earth; hence by Hypoth. II they depend on same causes. The forces fall off with distance as terrestrial gravity does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. to Prop. V — Gravity acts between all pairs and is mutual
rubrics_metrics.description: Igitur gravitas datur in Planetas universos... attractio omnis mutua est (per motus legem tertiam).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that every planet attracts every other and attraction is mutual (action = reaction). Examples: Jupiter attracts its satellites, Saturn and others likewise; mutual gravitation implies reaction forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VI (Theor. VI) — Weights proportional to quantity of matter; gravitational acceleration proportional to mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpora omnia in Planetas singulos gravitare, & pondera eorum in eundem quemvis Planetam, paribus distantiis à centro Planetæ, proportionalia esse quantitati materiæ in singulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pendulum experiments comparing different materials show equal fall/oscillation times, implying gravitational acceleration is proportional to amount of matter (mass). Uses argument from satellite motions and regularity to deduce proportionality of gravitational force to mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 1 to Prop. VI — Weight independent of shape and texture
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinc pondera corporum non pendent ab eorum formis & texturis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If weight depended on form, weights would vary for equal material — contrary to experiment. (Criterion: experimental observation rules out shape dependence.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 3 to Prop. VI — Necessity of vacuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Itaque Vacuum necessariò datur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all space were filled with fluid, less dense materials would not sink through denser, contradicting observed descent of bodies; thus vacuum must exist. (Criterion: theoretical implications must be consistent with the existence of vacuum.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 4 to Prop. VI — Gravity distinct from magnetism
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatem diversi generis esse à vi magnetica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnetic attraction behaves differently (selective attraction, can be turned on/off, falls off faster than inverse-square near the magnet); gravity is universal and distinct. (Criterion: distinguish different forces by their phenomenology and laws.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII (Theor. VII) — Gravity proportional to quantity of matter universally
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatem in corpora universa fieri, eamque proportionalem esse quantitati materiæ in singulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using planetary mutual attractions and composition of gravitational forces from parts, gravity of any body on another is proportional to amount of matter in it. (Reinforces universality and mass-proportionality.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII (Theor. VIII) — Inverse-square law for homogeneous spheres (sphere-sphere law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Globorum duorum in se mutuò gravitantium materia undique, in regionibus quæ à centris æqualiter distant, homogenea sit: erit pondus Globi alterutrius in alterum reciprocè ut quadratum distantiæ inter centra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After composing contributions of parts, deduce that two homogeneous spheres attract as if concentrated at their centers with inverse-square dependence. (Guides modelling planets/satellites as point masses for distance relations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 1 to Prop. VIII — Method to compare planetary weights and deduce masses/densities
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinc inveniri & inter se comparari possunt pondera corporum in diversos Planetas... pondera corporum in Solem, Jovem, Saturnum & Terram forent ad invicem ut 1, 1/1100, 1/2360 & 1/28700 respectively (example numeric ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From periods, apparent diameters, and satellite eclipses one can compute relative weights, masses and densities of planets; explicit numerical method and sample results provided. (Criterion: theory must enable computation of planetary masses/densities consistent with observations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX (Theor. IX) — Decrease of gravity with distance (accounting for density variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatem pergendo à superficiebus Planetarum deorsum decrescere in ratione distantiarum à centro quam proximè.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If planetary matter were uniformly dense the proposition would follow exactly; deviations are bounded by possible inhomogeneous density. (Criterion: inverse-square law holds to high accuracy, with corrections limited by interior density variations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X (Theor. X) — Longevity of planetary motion; negligible resistance in celestial medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus Planetarum in Cœlis diutissimè conservari posse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resistance computed from pendulum and fluid arguments shows extremely small fractional loss of motion in large bodies; as one ascends to heavens medium density (and resistance) diminishes enormously so planetary motions persist. (Criterion: account for conservation of planetary motion given minimal resistive forces.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XI (Theor. XI) — Common centre of gravity remains at rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Commune centrum gravitas Terræ Solis & Planetarum omnium quiescere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By laws of motion and mutual gravitation the common centre either remains at rest or moves uniformly; if it moved uniformly then world-center hypothesis would be undermined. (Criterion: modelling must respect conservation of center of mass/momentum.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XII (Theor. XII) — Sun's motion constrained near the common centre of gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Solem motu perpetuo agitari sed nunquam longe recedere à communi gravitatis centro Planetarum omnium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given relative masses and distances (Sun much more massive than planets), the Sun moves but never far from the common centre of gravity; modelling of planetary motion must reflect this small solar motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIII (Theor. XIII) — Derivation of Keplerian ellipses and area law from gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetæ moventur in Ellipsibus umbilicum habentibus in centro Solis, & radiis ad centrum illud ductis areas describunt temporibus proportionales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If planetary forces are central to the Sun and inverse-square, and mutual interactions are negligible, orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus and areas are swept proportionally to time — theoretical derivation reproduces Kepler's laws (with perturbative corrections when planets interact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIV (Theor. XIV) — Stability of aphelia and nodes (to first approximation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orbium Aphelia & Nodi quiescunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aphelia and orbital planes are fixed by earlier propositions; planetary and cometary interactions produce only small perturbations that can be neglected for many purposes. (Criterion: theory should predict small perturbations and near-stability of orbital elements.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Props. XV–XVI — Procedures to determine orbital dimensions, excentricities and aphelia
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XV: Invenire Orbium transversas diametros... Prop. XVI: Invenire Orbium Excentricitates & Aphelia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives procedural prescriptions: use ratios of periods (sesquialtera) and the sum of masses, and earlier propositions to compute transverse diameters, excentricities, and aphelia from observations. (Criterion: provide algorithms linking observations to orbital parameters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVII (Theor. XVI) — Diurnal rotation and lunar libration
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetarum motus diurnos uniformes esse, & librationem Lunæ ex ipsius motu diurno oriri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the first law of motion and rotational considerations: uniform diurnal rotation of planets explains lunar libration in longitude; libration in latitude arises from axial inclination. (Criterion: explanations of libration and rotation must follow from rotational motion assumptions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVIII (Theor. XVII) — Rotational flattening (axes smaller than diameters perpendicular to them)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axes Planetarum dimetris quæ ad eosdem axes normaliter ducuntur minores esse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of diurnal circular motion and centrifugal effects, bodies attain spheroidal shapes with equatorial bulge; observation (Cassini, Flamsteed) supports Jupiter's polar flattening. (Criterion: account for oblateness due to rotation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIX (Prob. II) — Computation of planet axis-to-diameter ratio and centrifugal/gravitational balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire proportionem axis Planetæ ad diametros eidem perpendiculares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives computational method: relate centrifugal force from diurnal motion to gravity to obtain axis ratio (example: if axis:diameter = 100:101 then centrifugal to gravity ratio computed and gravities at poles/equator compared). (Criterion: derive planetary figure from dynamics quantitatively.)
